records.name_note: Given as "Brassica oleracea var. gemmifera," the traditional botanical-variety form. NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox and RHS both use the modern cultivar-group convention for this crop, titling it "Brassica oleracea Brussels Sprouts Group (Brussels Sprouts, Gemmifera Group, Sprouts)" -- i.e. "Brassica oleracea Gemmifera Group." Both forms name the identical plant; the Group designation is recorded as the accepted name here since it is how the two authoritative sources on record (NC State, RHS) currently classify it.
unknowns: night_f_min/night_f_max: no source on the approved list gives a specific nighttime temperature range for Brussels sprouts.
humidity_need/humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max: none of the extension sources address ambient humidity requirements for this outdoor crop.

light_fc_min/light_fc_good: sources describe sun exposure only as duration categories (full sun / part shade hours), never as footcandle intensity -- used outdoor_sun_exposure instead per field notes.

toxic_to_pets/toxicity_detail: NC State's Plant Toolbox tags this species '#problem for horses' but gives no explanation of the hazard, mechanism, or whether it extends to common household pets (cats/dogs) -- too vague and non-specific to record as a pet-toxicity fact.

fertilize_interval_days/fertilize_active_months/fertilize_strength: UGA Extension states to 're-fertilize with nitrogen every 3 to 4 weeks' but only gives the interval in weeks (not a day count), and no source gives a month-of-year fertilizing schedule or a dilution/strength recommendation; declined to silently convert weeks to a days figure that would not literally appear in the quote.

soil_drainage: NC State's Plant Toolbox tags this species 'Good Drainage' and 'Moist' as short standalone attribute labels without enough surrounding sentence context to confidently place it on the fast/moderate/moisture_retentive scale.
water_check_depth_cm/water_growing_days_est/water_dormant_days_est: no source gives a soil-check depth or a day-count watering interval estimate for this crop.
cool_rest_note: no source addresses a dormancy or cool-rest period for this annual/biennial vegetable crop.

scientific_name_accepted — removed on audit: The value 'Brassica oleracea Gemmifera Group' is not what its own cited quote establishes. The NC State citation's quote reads 'Brassica oleracea Brussels Sprouts Group (Brussels Sprouts, Gemmifera Group, Sprouts)' -- confirmed verbatim on the live NC State page, where the page's own scientific/title designation is 'Brassica oleracea Brussels Sprouts Group,' and 'Gemmifera Group' appears only inside the parenthetical list of common-name synonyms alongside 'Brussels Sprouts' and 'Sprouts,' not as NC State's accepted scientific designation. The record extracted the parenthetical synonym and spliced it onto 'Brassica oleracea' to build a string ('Brassica oleracea Gemmifera Group') that NC State itself never uses -- if anything, the literal NC State-supported accepted name would be 'Brassica oleracea Brussels Sprouts Group.' The name_note compounds this by asserting NC State AND RHS 'both use... titling it "Brassica oleracea Brussels Sprouts Group..." -- i.e. "Brassica oleracea Gemmifera Group"' -- but I confirmed RHS's actual title format is 'Brassica oleracea (Gemmifera Group),' not 'Brassica oleracea Brussels Sprouts Group,' so the note's claim that both sources use that exact quoted title is false, and the single citation actually attached to this field does not literally support the value stored in it.

records.name_note: Given name "Brassica oleracea var. capitata" refers to the same cultivated cabbage as the cultivar-group designation "Brassica oleracea (Capitata Group)" used by current extension and garden references (Clemson HGIC, Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder). Modern horticultural sources for this crop consistently use the Capitata Group format rather than the older varietal epithet, so that form is recorded as scientific_name_accepted at the same binomial+group specificity level given. This is not a synonym correction in the taxonomic-rank sense, just the naming convention current sources use.
unknowns: night_f_min/night_f_max: no admissible source gives a nighttime-specific temperature figure for cabbage (only general/day growing temperatures were found).

light_fc_min, light_fc_good: garden sources describe sun exposure only as a duration/category (full sun, hours/day), never as footcandle intensity, per field guidance to use outdoor_sun_exposure instead for a garden crop.

soil_drainage: sources describe soil qualitatively as 'well-drained' (Clemson, UGA, MOBOT) but none categorize it as fast/moderate/moisture_retentive precisely enough to assign one of the enum values with confidence.

day_f_min — removed on audit: Verified against the live Clemson HGIC page: the quoted sentence 'They grow best at temperatures of 60 to 65 °F' follows directly from 'Cabbage (...) and Chinese cabbage (...) are cool-season vegetables that should be grown in early spring or fall,' so 'They' refers to both crops jointly. Chinese cabbage is Brassica rapa (Pekinensis Group), a different species from this record's Brassica oleracea cabbage. The citation is a shared two-species statement, not evidence specific to cabbage alone, so day_f_min=60 is sourced to a claim broader than 'this species specifically.'

day_f_max — removed on audit: Same defect as day_f_min: the source quote 'They grow best at temperatures of 60 to 65 °F' is confirmed (via direct fetch of the Clemson page) to be a joint statement covering both cabbage and Chinese cabbage (Brassica rapa) together, not a cabbage-specific figure. Attributing this shared range as this species' day_f_max over-reaches on species specificity.

chill_damage_f — removed on audit: The Clemson quote 'Mature cabbages can withstand temperatures as low as 18 to 20 °F' establishes a survival/tolerance threshold for MATURE plants only — it does not say damage begins at 18°F, only that mature cabbage survives down to that range. The record applies 18 as chill_damage_f for the crop generally (the 'mature plants' qualifier from the claim label is not reflected in the field itself), which risks understating cold-damage risk to young transplants/seedlings, which are typically less cold-hardy than mature heads. The corroborating UMD source also gives a different low end (15°F vs Clemson's 18°F), underscoring that 'withstand as low as X' is an approximate survival boundary from these sources, not a precise, agreed-upon damage-onset temperature as the field name implies.

direct_sun_hours_max — removed on audit: The only citation for the '10' value is a UMD sentence: 'Full sun requires direct light at least 6 hours/day; prefers 8 - 10 hours/day.' I fetched the live UMD page and confirmed this is a generic definition of the term 'full sun' (the kind of boilerplate glossary line UMD extension reuses across many vegetable grow-guides), not a carrot-specific finding about how many hours carrots need. It never mentions carrots. This is exactly the genus/general-statement failure mode the audit brief calls out: a category definition ('full sun means 8-10 hrs') is being used as if it were species-specific data.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: The claim label adds the parenthetical '(well-drained, not moisture-retentive)', but the cited RHS quote only says 'Grow in light, well-drained, deep soils in full sun' — it never says anything about moisture retention. I fetched the live RHS page and its own structured 'Drainage' field for this exact plant reads 'Moist but well-drained or Well-drained' — i.e. RHS itself allows for moisture-retentive well-drained soil. The 'not moisture-retentive' claim is therefore unsupported by the cited quote and actually contradicted by the source's own structured data, and it sits in tension with the record's own water_regime=keep_moist (which requires the soil to hold moisture).

day_f_min — removed on audit: Populated from Clemson's 'grow best at average temperatures between 60 and 65 °F.' I fetched the live Clemson page and confirmed this figure is explicitly a general/ambient average (distinguished in the same passage from the separately-stated soil-germination temperature), with no day-vs-night breakdown given anywhere on the page. The record's own unknowns list even admits 'sources give only one combined grows-best temperature band... without separating day from night readings' — yet that same undifferentiated figure was still assigned specifically to day_f_min rather than left unknown alongside night_f_min, which the researcher does leave null. Treating an unqualified average as a daytime-specific minimum is an unsupported category assignment.

day_f_max — removed on audit: Same defect as day_f_min: the Clemson 60-65°F figure is confirmed (via live fetch) to be a general average temperature with no day/night distinction, yet it was mapped onto the day-specific field while night_f_max was correctly left null — an inconsistent application of the same ambiguous data point.

scientific_name_accepted — removed on audit: The citation's quote — 'Carrots are a commonly cultivated, cool-season vegetable in the carrot family (Apiaceae) and are native to central Asia and Afghanistan.' — is pure background/origin text and never states or establishes that Daucus carota subsp. sativus is the accepted name; it doesn't even contain the scientific name. Per the audit checklist's own test ('does the quote ACTUALLY state this value, or does it merely sound related'), this quote fails: it merely comes from a page whose title/URL happens to carry the name, which is not the same as the quoted text substantiating the naming claim. (The name value itself is populated and plausibly correct — RHS independently uses the same name — so this is a citation-quality defect on the field's evidence, not necessarily a wrong value.)

scientific_name_accepted — removed on audit: The record keeps the given name 'Beta vulgaris subsp. vulgaris' as accepted purely on absence-of-contradiction reasoning, which the record's own name_note admits: none of the three admissible sources that give a scientific name for Swiss chard actually uses 'subsp. vulgaris' for it. NC State and Missouri Botanical Garden (confirmed by direct fetch) both classify it informally as 'Beta vulgaris (Leaf Beet Group)', and University of Maryland Extension (confirmed by direct fetch) names it 'Beta vulgaris var. cicla' -- a different infraspecific rank than subspecies. No admissible citation affirmatively supports 'subsp. vulgaris' as the accepted name for this specific variety; 'no source contradicts it' is not the same as a source confirming it, and per the audit's own standard silence/non-contradiction should not be read as confirmation.

name_note — removed on audit: name_note attributes a specific claim to RHS -- "RHS notes the 'Swiss' name is a 19th-century seed-catalog invention to distinguish chard from French spinach, even though the plant is Mediterranean in origin" -- but I fetched the cited RHS page (rhs.org.uk/vegetables/chard/grow-your-own) directly and it contains no mention of '19th century,' 'seed catalog,' 'French spinach,' or 'Mediterranean' anywhere in its text. That exact origin story ('The name Swiss Chard originated in Europe in the 19th century as a way of distinguishing chard from French spinach in seed catalogs. Both chard and beet spinach were domesticated in the Mediterranean area...') is instead verbatim text from the Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder page, which is cited elsewhere in this same record for a different claim. This is a source misattribution inside the naming justification, not a minor imprecision.

soil_base — removed on audit: The citation's claim label asserts 'grown in prepared garden soil, not a specialty potting mix,' but the quoted MOBOT text only describes soil texture and fertility ('moist, light, fertile, organically-rich, well-drained soils in full sun to light shade') and says nothing about containers or potting mix -- that contrast is an inference added past what the quote states. is_houseplant — removed on audit: Verified against the live NC State Plant Toolbox page: collards are never called a houseplant or described for indoor growing anywhere on the page. The cited evidence is a 'Container' entry under Landscape Location and a '#container plant' tag, sitting alongside other outdoor landscape-location tags ('Coastal', 'Border', 'Mass Planting', '#edible garden', '#full sun tolerant'). That is a statement that collards can be grown in an outdoor container, not that the species is a houseplant. The record's own citation even concedes this ('container growing listed as a landscape use'). This also contradicts the record's own other fields: outdoor_sun_exposure is full_sun (6+ hours direct sunlight, per the same NC State page) and soil_base is garden_bed -- neither is compatible with typical indoor houseplant siting. is_houseplant should be false.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: The citation's own quote is 'Good Drainage' (confirmed present verbatim on the NC State Plant Toolbox page as a Drainage tag), but the field was recorded as 'moderate.' The researcher's own parenthetical even flags this ('source states "Good Drainage"') and then assigns a different, weaker category anyway with no stated conversion rule. The value contradicts the source it cites; it should reflect 'good'/well-drained, not 'moderate.'

toxic_to_pets — removed on audit: Confirmed directly against the NC State Plant Toolbox page: the '#problem for horses' tag appears only in the page's flat tag list at the bottom, with no accompanying Toxicity/Poison section anywhere on the page -- no toxic principle, no symptoms, no plant part, no severity, nothing explaining what 'problem' means (could be toxicity, could be colic/bloat risk from overconsumption of brassicas, could be something else entirely). That is thin, undefined evidence for 'toxic' at all. Separately, 'toxic_to_pets' as a field is conventionally understood to mean common companion animals (cats/dogs), and horses are the only animal this source addresses -- the citation and toxicity_detail both admit 'no cat/dog data.' Using an unexplained horse-only tag to set toxic_to_pets = true over-extends a source that doesn't clearly establish toxicity for any pet this field is normally read to cover. (toxicity_detail's prose is honest about the horse-only scope, but the boolean itself is not adequately supported and will mislead a cat/dog owner reading only the flag.)

soil_base — removed on audit: The cited Clemson quote -- 'Collards may be grown in a variety of soils' -- is a statement about soil texture/type tolerance (clay, sandy, loam, etc.), not about planting structure or location. It doesn't actually establish 'garden_bed' as opposed to any other soil_base category, and is in tension with the same record's own NC State citation showing 'Container' listed as a valid landscape location for this species. The claim label leads with the right field name but the quote doesn't support the specific value chosen.

scientific_name_accepted — removed on audit: scientific_name_accepted IS populated (not the null-despite-name_note defect), but the reasoning in name_note that arrives at it overreaches. I fetched both cited pages directly. Clemson's actual sentence is "Sweet corn (Zea mays var. rugosa) is a warm-season crop..." -- it never mentions "saccharata" anywhere. UMD's sentence is "Sweet corn (Zea mays convar. saccharata var. rugosa) is a variety of maize...". name_note asserts "Both admissible-domain sources agree on including the 'rugosa' varietal epithet alongside 'saccharata'" -- that is false for Clemson, whose quote supports 'rugosa' REPLACING 'saccharata' in its usage, not 'rugosa' appearing alongside it. More fundamentally, both quotes are incidental parenthetical species labels used to introduce the crop in a growing guide, not statements from either source asserting what the taxonomically 'accepted' name is. Neither source is a taxonomic authority (e.g., USDA PLANTS/ITIS/GRIN), so treating an incidental wording difference between two Extension fact sheets as grounds to construct and prefer a novel composite trinomial ('Zea mays convar. saccharata var. rugosa') over the given, more standard name ('Zea mays var. saccharata') is not actually supported by what the cited quotes say.

is_houseplant — removed on audit: The only citation backing is_houseplant=false is the NC State quote 'Cowpea or long bean is a tropical, annual climber in the bean family (Fabaceae) that is native to tropical Africa but cultivated throughout warm areas of the world.' That sentence never mentions indoor growing, containers, or houseplant use in either direction -- it is a generic habit/origin description, not a statement that the species is (or isn't) grown as a houseplant. The claim label's own parenthetical ('no source describes indoor/container growing') admits this is an absence-of-evidence inference dressed up as a sourced fact rather than a quote that actually states the value. Per check #1 (does the quote actually state this value, or does it merely sound related?), this fails -- it merely sounds related. The underlying value is plausibly true for a field bean crop, but the citation does not establish it, so the field should have been left null/unknown rather than asserted as false with a citation implying direct source support.

normalizations: 2026-08-21: landed with zero manual fixes. Two of the eight subagent researchers (Brussels Sprouts, Sweet Corn) ran with the workflow's safety classifier rate-limited, so both were read in full by hand rather than trusting the loader pass alone. Both held up: Brussels Sprouts' audit independently verified NC State's and RHS's actual page titles and correctly killed a spliced-together scientific name neither source uses; Sweet Corn's audit re-fetched Clemson's page and caught that its own name_note misread 'rugosa replacing saccharata' as 'rugosa alongside saccharata', correctly nulling a fabricated composite trinomial. The four Brassica oleracea varieties in this batch (Brussels Sprouts, Cabbage, Cauliflower, Collards) share pages and boilerplate on some source sites -- the audit caught cauliflower's 'full sun' citation as boilerplate copied verbatim from UMD's broccoli page, and caught three separate 'average temperature' figures being misapplied to the day-only field across cabbage, carrot and cauliflower. The one numeric flag from a first-pass check (Swiss Chard's water_growing_days_est=7, quote says 'per week') is the same class of unambiguous unit conversion already accepted in prior batches.
